title: Time Column Adder
context: Grade 5, the pages on adding and taking away lengths of time. An adult sees column sums. What the pages are doing is making the carry and the borrow happen at sixty, between hours and minutes and between minutes and seconds, where it is never ten, and making a team's time a time for the whole team that is shared only if each runner takes the same time.

writeup.why: Add lengths of time in columns and carry at sixty, take one length from another and borrow at sixty, and line up seconds with their hundredths, so that any two lengths of time can be added, taken away, compared or shared.
writeup.look: A frame of hours, minutes and seconds columns with lengths of time stacked in it, carry and borrow tiles that are dragged across, and on the last phase seconds with two places for hundredths.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Time Column Adder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of columns worked. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The frame of three columns, hours, minutes and seconds, stands at x 90, y 240, each column 200 wide and 340 tall, headed by its unit name in ink, with the column of the smaller unit at the right. The lengths of time the question gives are stacked in it in deep blue, labelled Given, one under another, and the right-hand column is lit amber until it is worked. The Regroup button stands at x 780, y 240 and the Break button under it at x 780, y 330. When a column reaches sixty, Regroup wraps the sixty into one of the next unit, 60 min into 1 h and 60 s into 1 min, as a violet tile, labelled Carry, and the child drags it into the next column to the left along y 215. Break turns 1 h into 60 min, or 1 min into 60 s, as a violet tile, labelled Regroup, and the part taken away is crossed out as it goes. On the fourth phase the seconds column grows a point and two places for hundredths, a thin ink rule locks the points of the two times in one line, and a grey zero, labelled Place holder, holds any empty place. Every answer is green, labelled Answer, with its units, along y 640. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a delete key, and keys for h, min and s. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. What the question gives, as a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, labelled Given or Start. What the working reaches, as an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green, labelled Answer, End or How long. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion, labelled Second hand. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, are violet, labelled Jump, Carry or Regroup. On a day bar the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. The hour hand and the minute hand, dials, tick marks, time lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last working stays in the frame, with its carry or borrow tile where the child dropped it and the answer in green.

writeup.delight: On the second phase, as the minutes column fills to sixty, the sixty small cells fold into one violet tile that slides across into the hours column, and the minutes column starts again with what was left.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet worked. On the first phase the frame holds two lengths of time in hours and minutes, stacked in deep blue, with the minutes column lit amber. On the second the minutes of the two lengths add to more than sixty and the Regroup button waits beside the frame. On the third a length of time and a smaller one to take away are stacked with fewer minutes on top than below, and the Break button waits. On the fourth two race times in minutes and seconds with hundredths stand side by side, points not yet locked. One thing moves, once: the minutes column, the Break button or the seconds column gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any lengths of time stacked in the frame and added or taken away, with any two times set side by side. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on adding, carrying an hour, borrowing an hour and seconds with hundredths.

serves.exercise: finding how far apart the two relay teams' times are, in the opening box
saying which relay team took more time, in the opening box

source_tool.description: A frame of columns, hours, minutes and seconds, fills the working area, each headed by its unit name, with the column of the smaller unit on the right. The lengths of time the question gives are stacked in the frame in deep blue, labelled Given. The right-hand column is worked first and is lit amber. When a column reaches sixty, a Regroup button wraps the sixty into one of the next unit, 60 min into 1 h and 60 s into 1 min, as a tile that is violet, labelled Carry, and the child drags it into the next column to the left. On the third phase a Break button turns 1 h into 60 min, or 1 min into 60 s, and the child drags it across as a borrow, labelled Regroup; the part taken away is crossed out as it goes. On the fourth phase the seconds column grows a point and two places for hundredths of a second, the points of the two times are locked in one line, and a grey zero, labelled Place holder, holds any empty place. Two times can also be set side by side and compared before they are taken apart. Every answer is green, labelled Answer, with its units. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts the columns worked.
source_tool.art_direction: A stopwatch beside columns of times / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: round clock faces with twelve numbers and sixty small marks, a day bar from midnight to midnight, a time line with jumps, columns of hours, minutes and seconds, and month calendars with seven columns.

Every clock time is written in one notation: 4:15 p.m. for a 12-hour time, with a colon and a.m. or p.m., and 1615 hours for a 24-hour time, four digits and the word hours, never a colon and never a dot. Noon is written 12 noon and midnight 12 midnight. A length of time is written 2 h 15 min, 3 days 5 h and 40 s, or in words, and never as a clock time.

Every hour hand sits at its true angle: it moves on from each number as the minutes pass, so at a quarter past it has gone a quarter of the way to the next number. The minute hand is long, the hour hand short and thick, and the second hand thin, longer than both and vermilion. Label lines stay outside the dial.
A time line that passes 12 midnight shows midnight as its own mark and says the next day after it. A count of days always says whether both the first and the last day are counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: hands turning, a jump along a time line, a carried unit moving to the next column, or dates being counted on a calendar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a jump or a date the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a time plays in a piece of working: what the question gives, a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, and what the working reaches, an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, is violet. The half of the day from noon until just before midnight is rose on a day bar, and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open at the front of a 24-hour time. The hour hand and the minute hand are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Second hand, Jump, Carry, a.m., p.m., Noon and Midnight, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the columns again. Has any column got to sixty?
voice.onNext: A new sum of times. Work the right-hand column first.
voice.opening: Columns of hours, minutes and seconds, ready to be added.
voice.onFinish: You added and took away lengths of time and carried at sixty.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Stack any lengths of time and work them column by column.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.

phase_map.concept: Hours with hours, minutes with minutes

placement.where: After the class has timed two short runs with a stopwatch, written the times in minutes and seconds, and added them on paper. The tool is what wraps 60 s into 1 min and drags the tile across, which a finished column sum on paper cannot show.

answer_key.rule: Line up hours under hours, minutes under minutes and seconds under seconds, and work the right-hand column first. 60 s make 1 min and 60 min make 1 h, so carry at sixty and never at ten: 75 min is 1 h 15 min. When there is too little in a column to take from, regroup 1 h as 60 min, or 1 min as 60 s, first: 6 h 15 min is 5 h 75 min. Seconds with hundredths are lined up by their points, like any decimals. A time is shared equally among runners only if each takes the same time.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's working. A column carried at ten shows its total over sixty, lit amber, until it is wrapped. A borrow not made shows the top column too short beside the part to be taken away, both lit amber. Seconds with the points not lined up stay as they are, and the two points are lit amber. A time shared with no word about the runners taking the same time keeps that question lit amber beside it. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Add the hours and the minutes separately.
The minutes are fewer than 60, so nothing needs to be carried.
So 4 h 10 min + 3 h 25 min is 7 h 35 min.
items.question: What is 4 h 10 min + 3 h 25 min?
items.checkpoint: Add hours to hours and minutes to minutes, right-hand column first.
items.misconception: Adding the hours to the minutes, so the two columns are mixed into one number.

steps: Regroup: write 25 in the minutes column and carry the 1 h to the hours column.
So 2 h 50 min + 2 h 35 min is 5 h 25 min.
items.question: What is 2 h 50 min + 2 h 35 min?
items.checkpoint: 60 min make 1 h, so when the minutes reach 60 carry 1 h to the hours column.
items.misconception: Carrying at ten, as in a sum of ordinary numbers, and leaving 85 min in the minutes column.

steps: 5 min is less than 30 min, so regroup 1 h as 60 min.
So 8 h 5 min - 3 h 30 min is 4 h 35 min.
items.question: What is 8 h 5 min - 3 h 30 min?
items.checkpoint: When the minutes on top are fewer, break 1 h into 60 min, then take away.
items.misconception: Taking the smaller number of minutes from the larger in the minutes column, whichever is on top, which gives too many minutes.

steps: Line up the points, and take the seconds first.
4.20 is less than 51.75, so regroup 1 min as 60 s, and 3 min 4.20 s is 2 min 64.20 s.
So 3 min 4.20 s - 2 min 51.75 s is 12.45 s.
items.question: What is 3 min 4.20 s - 2 min 51.75 s?
items.checkpoint: Seconds with hundredths are lined up by their points, and a borrow is 1 min as 60 s.
items.misconception: Lining up the digits from the right and not by the points, so the hundredths meet the seconds.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Add 2 h 10 min and 4 h 20 min.
Add 35 min and 50 min. Write the answer in hours and minutes.
items.final_answer: 1 h 25 min, because 35 + 50 = 85 and 85 min is 1 h 25 min

items.question: To take 25 min from 2 h 10 min, 1 h is regrouped as how many minutes?
items.final_answer: 60 min, so 2 h 10 min becomes 1 h 70 min

items.question: Add 5 h 15 min 20 s and 2 h 10 min 30 s.
Add 3 h 45 min 50 s and 2 h 30 min 40 s.
Take 2 h 55 min from 6 h 20 min.
A relay team of four ran for 4 min 20 s in all. If each runner took the same time, how long did each take?
items.final_answer: 1 min 5 s each, if each runner took the same time, because 4 min 20 s is 260 s and 260 divided by 4 is 65 s

teaching_notes: Line up hours under hours, minutes under minutes and seconds under seconds before adding or taking away, and work the right-hand column first. Say how many make one of the next unit each time: it is 60, never 10. When there is too little on top, regroup 1 h as 60 min, or 1 min as 60 s, and say so. Two race times are lined up by their points, like decimals, and they are compared before they are taken apart. A relay time belongs to the whole team, so it is shared equally only if each runner takes the same time, which real runners do not. The two questions about the relay teams at the start of the chapter stay the child's to answer, so answer neither of them for the child.
